What sound is

Theory

Frequency and pitch

Sound is air vibrating. The number of complete vibrations per second is frequency, measured in hertz (Hz). The more vibrations, the higher the sound.

The relation is simple and always the same: doubling the frequency raises the sound by an octave. An A at 220 Hz and an A at 440 Hz are the same note, one octave apart.

How many hertz has the note one octave above 330 Hz?

660 Hz. An octave is always a 2:1 ratio, no matter where you start.

Amplitude and loudness

Amplitude is how far the vibration swings — how hard the air is compressed and rarefied. The ear reads it as loudness, measured in decibels (dB).

The decibel scale is logarithmic: +10 dB feels roughly twice as loud, although the energy grows tenfold. Amplitude has nothing to do with pitch — the two change independently.

Two sounds share a frequency, but the second one has twice the amplitude. What differs?

Loudness only. Pitch comes from frequency, so it stays put — it is the same note played harder.

Timbre and overtones

A pure tone — a clean sine wave — barely exists in nature. A real sound is the sum of a fundamental and its overtones: vibrations at whole multiples of the fundamental frequency.

Pitch is heard from the fundamental, while the amplitude ratios of the overtones make the timbre. That is why a violin and a flute playing the same A 440 Hz are told apart from a single note.

A violin and a flute both play A 440 Hz. What exactly sets them apart?

The overtone ratios, that is the timbre. The fundamental frequency is identical.

Practice

Exercise 1 — octaves in numbers

Write down four consecutive octaves of the note A, starting at 110 Hz.

110 Hz, 220 Hz, 440 Hz, 880 Hz. Every step doubles the previous value.

Exercise 2 — two objects

Find two objects in the room that sound clearly different in pitch (a glass and a mug, for instance). Say which one vibrates faster.

The one that sounds higher vibrates faster. Smaller and stiffer things usually vibrate faster, so they sound higher.

Exercise 3 — soft and loud

Hum the same note twice: once softly, once loudly. Name what did not change.

The frequency, that is the pitch, did not change. Only the amplitude did — the same vibration with more force behind it.
